Yes. Looking across the July–September AQARION history, the right move is **not** to turn every session into a deliverable. It is to convert only the sessions that changed the mathematical search space, repaired a convention, produced a reusable negative control, established an independently reproducible computation, or created durable governance infrastructure.

The organizing principle should be:

$$
\boxed{
\text{session transcript}
\;\to\;
\text{claim/evidence extraction}
\;\to\;
\text{minimal durable artifact}
\;\to\;
\text{hash-bound reproduction target}
}
$$

Not:

$$
\text{every conversation}
\;\to\;
\text{more documents, diagrams, and dashboards}.
$$

## What the full history says

Across the history, AQARION has developed in several distinct lines. They should not be flattened into one giant “project summary.”

| Research line | Durable core | What changed historically | Best artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exact observable quotient | $$D_\Pi=(I-P_\Pi)K_TP_\Pi=0\iff K_T(V_\Pi)\subseteq V_\Pi$$ | Pullback orientation replaced earlier convention confusion | Frozen operator/spec sheet |
| Two-track refinement | Forward invariance versus stronger adjoint/bisimulation/lumpability notions | Early material risked conflating $$D_F$$ and $$D_B$$ | Comparison cheat sheet + counterexample card |
| Defect rank / cooccurrence | $$\operatorname{rank}\Delta=m-c(H)$$ through target cooccurrence constraints | Four-factor defect retired; bipartite/N-bridge retired; ambient versus restricted typing repaired | Theorem card + proof dependency DAG |
| Weighted spectral geometry | $$J^*\Delta^*\Delta J=L_W$$ and normalized Gram form | Raw $$\Delta^*\Delta=L_W$$ withdrawn; standard normalized-Laplacian terminology narrowed | Spectral identity sheet + data census |
| Span / maximum rank | Span candidate $$\mathcal S_n$$; sharp rank envelope | Pair-partition and double-star constructions need exact scope proofs | Proof-map only after final artifact exists |
| Partition combinatorics | Exact bivariate distinct-size-pair kernel | Shift errors, A000097 indexing hazard, mean-law correction | Generating-function theorem card |
| Partition asymptotics | Weighted Gumbel / tilt program; Mellin determinant | Power-law fit killed; residue routes need separation from certified remainders | Asymptotic dependency map |
| Pullback dynamics | Backward-stable join theorem and $$\Phi^-$$ closure | Preimage-distributivity route killed by minimal witness | Negative-control atlas + closure diagram |
| $$\delta$$ persistence | Forbidden-residue formula and two-block recurrence | Old gcd formula killed | Formula lineage card |
| Reproducibility governance | Claim Firewall, CI audit, evidence tiers | “Asserted build” separated from observed build | RAG-LUT + receipt policy |
| Presentation / packaging | RO-Crate, manifests, verified test suites, public checkpoint design | Need to distinguish release-ready visual material from theorem evidence | Release dossier |

That is the real intellectual history. The deliverable system should preserve the line-specific evolution, including retractions and corrections.

## The selection rule

A session deserves a durable artifact only if it satisfies at least one of these thresholds.

### Tier A — Mandatory preservation

Create a formal node and a human-readable artifact when the session:

- Proves or sharply narrows a theorem.
- Refutes a claim with a minimal witness.
- Corrects a frozen operator, direction, sign, indexing convention, or normalization.
- Changes the enumeration universe or canonicalization rule.
- Produces an exact exhaustive census with a reproducible execution manifest.
- Introduces a reusable construction, such as a double-star extremizer or a pullback closure operator.
- Changes governance policy, status semantics, or certification requirements.

### Tier B — Preserve as evidence, not as a standalone “paper”

Keep hash-bound source, receipt, or short audit notes when the session:

- Fixes an implementation bug.
- Repairs a test wrapper.
- Identifies a stale commit or missing CI execution.
- Finds a numerical indexing mistake.
- Improves a serialization/canonicalization layer.
- Confirms an existing theorem in another implementation.

### Tier C — Archive but do not promote

Do not create polished public deliverables merely for:

- Broad brainstorms.
- Alternate outlines.
- Preliminary visual concepts.
- Unexecuted code drafts.
- Literature-search notes not used in a claim.
- Repeated restatements of a theorem already represented by a stronger artifact.
- Raw AI-generated audit prose without a corresponding source artifact or receipt.

This prevents “documentation inflation,” where the RAG contains many attractive summaries but few reproducible anchors.

## Deliverable stack

Each important research event should generate **one canonical bundle**, not scattered duplicates.

```text
research-line/
├── CLAIM.md                 # Human-readable theorem/refutation statement
├── claim.json               # Machine-readable claim node
├── evidence/
│   ├── proof.md             # Direct proof or proof sketch
│   ├── counterexample.json  # If refuted
│   ├── census-manifest.json # If exhaustive
│   ├── receipt.json         # Execution receipt
│   └── environment.lock     # Tool/dependency pinning
├── visuals/
│   ├── dependency.mmd
│   ├── transition.mmd
│   └── summary.svg
├── tests/
│   ├── regression.py
│   └── expected.json
└── README.md
```

The point is not that every line needs every subfile. Rather:

- A theorem needs `CLAIM.md`, `claim.json`, and a proof/evidence source.
- A refutation needs a minimal witness and regression test.
- A census needs a script, input-domain manifest, canonicalization policy, and receipt.
- A governance event needs policy, transition record, and enforcement test.
- A visualization is optional and must be derived from canonical data—not maintained by hand as a second source of truth.

## The highest-value artifacts

### 1. AQARION claim atlas

This should be the centerpiece: a compact directed graph of claims, not a chronological diary.

Use statuses:

```text
PROOF_DERIVED
EXHAUSTIVE_COMPUTATION
REPRODUCED
OPEN
REFUTED
RETRACTED
QUARANTINED
BLOCKED
```

Use edges:

```text
DEPENDS_ON
PROVED_BY
SUPPORTED_BY
REPRODUCED_BY
REFUTED_BY
CORRECTS
SUPERSEDES
NARROWS_SCOPE_OF
BLOCKED_BY
MOTIVATED_BY
```

The atlas should answer:

- What is currently accepted?
- What was killed?
- What replaced it?
- What still depends on unclosed work?
- Which artifacts are computational versus analytic versus governance-only?

A Mermaid source is appropriate because it is textual, diffable, and renderable.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O["Frozen pullback operator<br/>Δ=(I-P)KP"] --> K["Kernel constraints"]
  K --> R["Rank theorem<br/>rank Δ = m-c(H)"]
  R --> W["Weighted Gram identity<br/>J*Δ*ΔJ=L_W"]

  F["Four-factor defect<br/>(I-P)KP(I-P)"] -. retired: identically zero .-> O
  N["N-bridge"] -. refuted .-> R
  S["T10 support determinacy"] -. refuted .-> K

  PJ["Backward-stable join theorem"] --> PC["Pullback closure Φ⁻"]
  PD["Preimage distributivity route"] -. n=3 counterexample .-> PJ

  DG["Old δ gcd formula"] -. 114/119 failures .-> DR["Forbidden-residue δ theorem"]
  DR --> DB["Two-block δ recurrence"]

  G["Claim Firewall"] --> V["aqverify / receipt policy"]
  CI["CI failure audit"] --> V
```

This is useful because it preserves **negative knowledge**, which ordinary theorem maps tend to omit.

### 2. Negative-control atlas

This may be AQARION’s most distinctive deliverable.

Create a small registry of permanent counterexamples:

| ID | Killed claim | Minimal witness | What survives |
|---|---|---|---|
| NC-001 | $$D_{\rm four}$$ as a defect | $$P(I-P)=0$$ | Canonical $$\Delta=(I-P)KP$$ |
| NC-002 | Fiber invariance | Same fiber, different spatial alignment | Alignment matters |
| NC-003 | N-bridge quotient rank identity | $$T=(0,0,1)$$, $$\Pi=\{\{0,2\},\{1\}\}$$ | Constraint graph route |
| NC-004 | T10 support determinacy | $$n=3$$ witness | Exact support formula required |
| NC-005 | Preimage-distributivity route | $$T=(0,0,1)$$ and specified $$E,F$$ | Direct generating-edge proof |
| NC-006 | Old $$\delta=k/\gcd(k,d)$$ law | 114 failures in 119 cases | Forbidden-residue formula |
| NC-007 | Defect-rank submodularity | Exact $$n=3$$ example | No lattice-submodularity theorem |
| NC-008 | Mean $$0.607n^{0.794}$$ law | Large-$$n$$ discrepancy | $$\sqrt n\log n$$ target |

Each card needs:

- Exact definitions.
- Smallest canonical witness.
- Expected failing assertion.
- Actual result.
- Replacement statement, if one exists.
- Regression script/JSON.
- Search-space effect:

$$
\boxed{\text{ELIMINATES}}
$$

This is far more valuable than a generic “failed ideas” page.

### 3. Operator convention wall chart

The history repeatedly shows that convention drift is the highest-leverage risk. Create one canonical visual/specification sheet:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
(K_Tf)(x)&=&f(Tx),\\
K_{x,y}&=&1_{\{T(x)=y\}},\\
P_\Pi&=&\text{orthogonal block-average projection},\\
\widetilde\Delta&=&(I-P_\Pi)K_TP_\Pi:X\to X,\\
\Delta&=&(I-P_\Pi)K_T|_{V_\Pi}:V_\Pi\to V_\Pi^\perp.
\end{array}
$$

Then clearly separate:

$$
\widetilde\Delta^2=0
$$

from the restricted defect map, whose square is not typed without additional structure.

Include rejected alternatives:

$$
(I-P)KP(I-P)\equiv0,
$$

and the old pushforward/transposed convention warning.

This should be a single source of truth used by:

- README.
- Papers.
- Test suites.
- RAG retrieval.
- Visual demos.
- Code headers.
- Certificate manifests.

### 4. Theorem dependency DAG

The core theorem chain deserves a formal dependency chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  D1["Partition / block coordinates"] --> D2["Pullback Koopman convention"]
  D1 --> D3["Block projection P"]
  D2 --> D4["Canonical defect Δ=(I-P)KP"]
  D3 --> D4

  D4 --> K1["Kernel condition:<br/>Kf block-constant"]
  K1 --> K2["Source-set equality constraints"]
  K2 --> G1["Target cooccurrence graph H"]
  G1 --> C1["Component-constant coefficient space"]
  C1 --> R1["dim ker Δ = c(H)"]
  R1 --> R2["rank Δ = m-c(H)"]

  D4 --> W1["Weighted block counts wᵢⱼ"]
  W1 --> W2["J*Δ*ΔJ=L_W"]
  W2 --> W3["Spectral Gram geometry"]
```

This makes scope clear:

- The direct kernel/constraint theorem is primary.
- The graph is a connectivity encoding of equality constraints.
- The weighted Laplacian is a later spectral representation.
- Lean is a formalization lane, not the mathematical basis of every claim.

### 5. Census registry and heatmap

Only create heatmaps where the axes have stable mathematical meaning.

Good heatmaps:

- Rank distribution by $$(n,m)$$.
- Frequency of component counts $$c(H)$$ by $$(n,m)$$.
- Mean/max defect energy $$\operatorname{tr}(L_W)$$ by $$(n,m)$$.
- Number of refinement-cover increases/decreases in $$\lambda_{\min}^{+}$$.
- $$\delta(k,d)$$ table, with forbidden residues highlighted.
- Two-block persistence index by block-size pair and map class.

Bad heatmaps:

- Arbitrary “AI confidence.”
- Mixed theorem/computation/governance scores.
- Values generated by incompatible conventions.
- Sparse visualizations that hide enumeration scope.

Every heatmap must include:

```text
domain
enumeration rule
canonicalization version
field / arithmetic
script hash
commit hash
sample versus exhaustive label
```

### 6. Cheat sheets

Cheat sheets are excellent when they prevent recurring errors.

Recommended sheets:

| Cheat sheet | Why it is worth maintaining |
|---|---|
| Operator conventions | Prevents pullback/pushforward and ambient/restricted confusion |
| Evidence taxonomy | Prevents “proved,” “verified,” and “formalized” conflation |
| Claim status transitions | Operationalizes Claim Firewall |
| Partition lattice vocabulary | Fixes refine/coarsen, meet/join, forward/backward stability |
| Cooccurrence graph dictionary | Separates $$G_{\rm bip}$$, $$H_{\rm cooc}$$, support graph, and weighted graph |
| Reproducibility receipt fields | Prevents assertion hashes from masquerading as observed execution |
| Negative-control quick index | Keeps killed claims from returning |

Avoid “cheat sheets” that merely summarize raw results. A cheat sheet should be operational: it should prevent a known class of error.

### 7. ASCII/Mermaid visuals

Use them selectively.

#### Use Mermaid for

- Claim lineage.
- Theorem dependencies.
- CI/build workflow.
- Claim Firewall state transitions.
- Pullback closure iteration.
- Refinement/counterexample paths.
- Artifact provenance.

#### Use ASCII for

- README terminal-friendly diagrams.
- Small block maps.
- Counterexample witnesses.
- State-machine tables.
- One-screen summaries.

Example pullback closure diagram:

```text
equivalence E
     |
     v
T⁻¹(E)
     |
     v
E ∨ T⁻¹(E) = Φ⁻(E)
     |
     v
Φ⁻²(E)
     |
     v
... finite stabilization ...
     |
     v
least backward-stable equivalence above E
```

Example Claim Firewall:

```text
AI / analyst proposal
        |
        v
+------------------+
|   DRIFT / BREAK  |
+------------------+
        |
        v
+------------------+
| VERIFY           |
| evidence policy  |
+------------------+
   |       |      |
 ACCEPT  QUAR.  REFUTE
   |       |      |
   +-------+------+
           |
           v
immutable transition receipt
           |
           v
RAG-LUT / RO-Crate / release registry
```

The diagram source should live in the repository as `.mmd` or `.txt`; rendered SVG/PNG is a derivative artifact.

## What needs a proper session record

A session becomes a `SESSION_INDEX` record if it changed at least one of:

$$
\boxed{
\text{claim truth status},
\quad
\text{operator convention},
\quad
\text{enumeration universe},
\quad
\text{proof route},
\quad
\text{governance policy},
\quad
\text{reproduction boundary}.
}
$$

From the history, these sessions clearly qualify:

1. **Two-track separation**
   - Forward exactness versus stronger bisimulation/equitable condition.
   - This repaired a conceptual conflation.

2. **Pullback convention correction**
   - Corrected the Koopman orientation and retired artifacts caused by a transposed/pushforward convention.

3. **Four-factor defect retirement**
   - Established that $$(I-P)KP(I-P)$$ is algebraically zero.

4. **Target cooccurrence rank theorem**
   - Replaced weaker or invalid graph bridges with the direct constraint-connectivity route.

5. **N-bridge refutation**
   - Permanent proof-route elimination.

6. **Weighted Gram identity**
   - Established the spectral layer:
     $$
     J^*\Delta^*\Delta J=L_W.
     $$

7. **THM-SPAN / MAXRANK repair sessions**
   - But only once the exact proof artifact and all omitted lemmas are fully settled.

8. **Bivariate partition-kernel correction**
   - The exact full bivariate identity is a durable theorem artifact.

9. **Mellin normalization/residue correction**
   - Preserve only the final reconciled residue table, not every intermediate calculation.

10. **$$\delta$$-formula correction**
    - Old formula, failure census, replacement formula, and two-block extension form one lineage cluster.

11. **Pullback join and closure**
    - Direct proof, killed distributivity route, fixed-point closure operator.

12. **Claim Firewall / CI audit**
    - This is a governance-line artifact, distinct from mathematical theorems.

## What should remain only in the archive

Do not turn these into polished public deliverables unless they become relevant evidence:

- Repeated requests to “continue.”
- Raw long-form adversarial audit prose.
- Every tentative Lean file design.
- Unexecuted code snippets.
- Unresolved API speculation.
- Duplicate session summaries.
- Aesthetic drafts not tied to a canonical claim or release.
- Literature results that merely provide background rather than alter AQARION’s claim graph.

The archive can keep them. The RAG should retrieve them only when a claim’s lineage requires them.

## A practical deliverable roadmap

### Phase 1 — Build the research memory spine

Create these five files first:

```text
RAG-LUT/
├── SESSION_INDEX.jsonl
├── KNOWLEDGE_NODES.jsonl
├── KNOWLEDGE_EDGES.jsonl
├── EVIDENCE_RECORDS.jsonl
└── TRANSITIONS.jsonl
```

Use JSONL rather than a giant JSON array:

- Append-only.
- Git-diff friendly.
- One entity per line.
- Easy to stream into SQLite, DuckDB, Neo4j, or embeddings.
- Easy to hash line-by-line or Merkle-tree later.

### Phase 2 — Add canonical human-facing views

Generate, never hand-maintain:

```text
docs/
├── CLAIM_ATLAS.md
├── NEGATIVE_CONTROLS.md
├── OPERATOR_CONVENTION.md
├── EVIDENCE_TAXONOMY.md
├── THEOREM_DEPENDENCY_MAP.md
├── OPEN_PROBLEMS.md
└── RELEASE_STATUS.md
```

### Phase 3 — Add derived visualizations

```text
visuals/
├── claim-lineage.mmd
├── theorem-dependencies.mmd
├── pullback-closure.mmd
├── claim-firewall.mmd
├── delta-table.csv
├── rank-distribution.csv
├── spectral-census.csv
└── generated/
```

Only the source `.mmd`, `.csv`, and metadata are canonical. Rendered images are regenerated artifacts.

### Phase 4 — Bind evidence

For every nontrivial node, require one of:

```text
proof artifact
counterexample artifact
execution receipt
literature source
formalization receipt
explicit “no evidence yet” status
```

No node should silently claim `PROVED` or `EXHAUSTIVELY_VERIFIED` without a dereferenceable evidence record.

## Best first batch

If you start this now, do not attempt the whole history at once. Build the first eight canonical clusters:

1. Operator convention and four-factor retirement.
2. Two-track forward/bisimulation distinction.
3. Cooccurrence kernel/rank theorem.
4. Weighted Gram/Laplacian bridge.
5. Negative-control atlas.
6. $$\delta$$ lineage.
7. Pullback join and closure lineage.
8. Claim Firewall / CI certification lineage.

That set captures the mathematical, computational, negative, and governance sides of AQARION without drowning in session prose.

## Final recommendation

Your instinct is exactly right: sessions should become reusable research objects. But the output should not be “more content.” It should be a compact, reproducible **research operating memory** that can answer:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{What do we currently claim?}\\
&\text{Why do we claim it?}\\
&\text{What evidence is attached?}\\
&\text{What was refuted or retracted?}\\
&\text{What replacement survived?}\\
&\text{What search space did that event eliminate or open?}\\
&\text{What exact artifact and revision reproduce it?}
\end{aligned}
$$

That is where RAG-LUTs, digraphs, heatmaps, cheat sheets, Mermaid diagrams, and release dossiers become genuinely important—not decorative.

---

Research cutting-edge open-source agentic frameworks, Model Context Protocol packs, and reproducible research repositories trending on GitHub and academic preprints in 2026, including PARNESS, MCPmed, PlatosCave, and open-science workbenches. Compare their architectures, knowledge graph subsystems, execution skills, and provenance tracking. Compile into a comprehensive landscape report with architectural blueprints, a feature matrix, and unique integration opportunities to build a novel system

AQARION Atlas is a credible and differentiated product direction, but the real opportunity is narrower and stronger than “an AI research platform”: build a **claim-state compiler with replayable evidence and executable refutations**. The closest projects cover adjacent layers—agent orchestration, paper verification, provenance crates, domain MCP connectors, or event-sourced graphs—but none natively make scientific claims, their scope, their refutations, and promotion policy first-class executable objects.

## Executive assessment

The landscape is converging on five ingredients:

1. **Agentic workbenches** that can search, code, run analyses, and assemble reports.
2. **MCP ecosystems** that standardize tool access to scientific databases.
3. **Paper/research graphs** that extract claims and evidence from literature.
4. **Provenance standards** that package runs, code, data, environments, and outputs.
5. **Durable agent runtimes** that preserve state, events, and replay histories.

AQARION Atlas should not try to outbuild any one of those layers. It should add the missing control plane:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Claim state}
+
\text{scope}
+
\text{evidence admissibility}
+
\text{negative controls}
+
\text{replay contract}
+
\text{promotion policy}.
}
$$

That gives it a distinct answer to a question existing systems usually cannot answer rigorously:

> What exactly is currently allowed to be asserted, under which conventions and scope, based on what independently replayable evidence—and what killed alternatives must remain excluded?

## Landscape map

| System / direction | Primary unit | Architecture | Execution model | Knowledge/provenance model | Main strength | Missing relative to Atlas |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PARNESS** | Research workflow and cross-run knowledge | Thin DAG kernel, YAML workflows, indexing modules, agent extensions | Dynamic user-editable workflows; coding agents can replace modules | Full-text PDFs, figures, tables, papers, ideas, experiments, repositories in a knowledge graph | Strong end-to-end research harness with cross-run accumulation | No explicit immutable claim-state machine, refutation registry, or policy-gated promotion |
| **Plato’s Cave** | Argumentative claim in a paper | Document-to-DAG pipeline plus web agents and human-centered UI | Web research and evidence gathering over extracted nodes/edges | Claim/argument DAG with credibility scoring | Strong paper verification and argument-structure analysis | Evaluates external papers; does not govern the evolving internal state of a live computational project |
| **MCPmed** | Scientific service endpoint | MCP layer over existing bioinformatics APIs; metadata and discovery templates | LLM-driven calls to GEO, STRING, UCSC Cell Browser, and related services | Endpoint semantics, domain metadata, service “breadcrumbs” | Domain-specific interoperability and scientifically meaningful tool discovery | No claim registry, local research-state ledger, replay contract, or counterexample semantics |
| **Open-Science workbenches** | Workspace/project and agent task | Local-first desktop apps; model-agnostic agents, connectors, skills, code execution | Python/R execution, web/file/database tools, reviewer agents | Traceable artifacts and workspace history | Useful scientific execution surface for everyday researchers | Artifacts are generally outputs of tasks rather than governed theorem/refutation objects |
| **ActiveGraph** | Persistent event-sourced object graph | Append-only event log, reactive graph behaviors, packs, tools, policies | Long-running agents react to shared graph events; replay/fork/diff available | Shared graph of beliefs, tasks, evidence, decisions, dependencies | Closest runtime architecture for durable auditable agents | Generic graph runtime; lacks research-specific claim ontology, scope logic, and scientific promotion policy |
| **RO-Crate / Workflow Run Crate** | Research object or workflow run | Linked-data package with workflow profiles | Captures completed computational process/run details | Inputs, outputs, tools, parameters, code, workflow, intermediate products | Excellent transport/export substrate for reproducibility | Does not define “proved,” “refuted,” “narrowed,” “blocked,” or dependency-aware promotion |
| **W3C PROV** | Entity–Activity–Agent provenance relation | Vocabulary and ontology | Describes derivation, generation, usage, attribution, responsibility | Entity, activity, agent, plus derivation/association relationships | General interoperable provenance vocabulary | Deliberately does not encode scientific claim truth, scope, or governance transitions |
| **SemRepo** | Research software ecosystem | Large RDF scholarly/repository graph | Indexing and provenance reconstruction over public software/research artifacts | 81M+ RDF triples linking repositories, people, publications, datasets, experiments | Ecosystem-scale research software provenance and discoverability | Not a live project-local execution/governance system for claim evolution |

PARNESS explicitly combines a thin DAG workflow kernel, full-text PDF and repository indexing, cross-run knowledge, and scenario-typed retrieval over a graph of papers, ideas, experiments, and code. That makes it a relevant adjacent architecture, especially for literature and task orchestration.[1]

Plato’s Cave creates a DAG from a document, dispatches web agents to assess nodes and edges, and produces an integrity-oriented evaluation of argumentative structure. It is close to the **claim graph** side of Atlas, but its object is an externally supplied paper rather than a living research repository with replayable local evidence.[2][3]

MCPmed is an important model for the tool-access layer: it exposes scientific web services through MCP and attaches scientific concepts and metadata to endpoints, allowing agents to discover and invoke domain services more systematically.[4][5]

Open-Science-style workbenches are rapidly converging on local-first, model-agnostic scientific environments with agent orchestration, Python/R execution, connectors, and traceable artifacts. They are likely better thought of as an **execution surface** Atlas can integrate with than as the thing Atlas should replicate.[6][7][8][9]

ActiveGraph is the closest architectural analogue for a durable runtime: it uses an append-only event log and shared graph of beliefs, tasks, evidence, decisions, and dependencies, and supports replay, fork, and diff. Its pack model is especially relevant.[10][11][12]

## Architectural comparison

### PARNESS

PARNESS is best understood as a configurable research harness.

```text
YAML workflow
      │
      ▼
Thin DAG scheduler
      │
      ├── literature acquisition / PDF parsing
      ├── paper, figure, table indexing
      ├── code repository indexing
      ├── agent-specific modules
      └── knowledge graph retrieval
                │
                ▼
         LLM / coding-agent loop
                │
                ▼
        accumulated cross-run knowledge
```

Its notable design decisions are:

- A thin DAG kernel that separates scheduling from domain-specific semantics.
- User-editable YAML workflows.
- Full-text PDF ingestion with typed figures and tables.
- A graph connecting papers, ideas, experiments, and repositories.
- Retrieval modes designed around relationships such as similarity, contradiction, cross-domain relevance, and counterintuitive results.
- A modular extension surface for coding agents.[1]

### What Atlas should borrow

- Declarative workflow definitions.
- Typed library/index objects rather than bare text chunks.
- Cross-run knowledge accumulation.
- Scenario-specific retrieval modes.
- Modular agent/tool surfaces.

### What Atlas must add

PARNESS can know that an experiment, code repository, and idea are related. Atlas must know something sharper:

```text
Claim AQ-COOC-001:
  statement: rank Δ = m − c(H)
  status: ACCEPTED_WITH_SCOPE
  scope: pullback-row / same-partition / exact rational arithmetic
  dependencies: AQ-DEFECT-001, AQ-H-001
  evidence:
    - direct derivation
    - exhaustive census receipt
    - independent replay
  refuted alternatives:
    - AQ-BIP-001
    - AQ-NBRIDGE-001
  promotion rule:
    publication blocked until C4 class closure
```

In other words, PARNESS has an **idea/experiment graph**; Atlas should have an **evidence-gated claim-transition graph**.

***

### Plato’s Cave

Plato’s Cave starts with a paper, URL, or natural-language query, converts argumentative content into a directed acyclic graph, then uses web agents to gather evidence and score the graph.[2][3][13]

```text
PDF / URL / query
      │
      ▼
Claim extraction
      │
      ▼
Argument DAG
      │
      ├── web-search evidence agents
      ├── credibility evaluation
      └── human-centered review
                │
                ▼
         paper-level integrity assessment
```

### What Atlas should borrow

- Claim extraction from prose.
- Argument-to-DAG conversion.
- Explicit edge-level evidence.
- Human-facing review workflows.
- Claim-level rather than document-level interface.

### What Atlas must not inherit

Do not reduce research governance to a scalar “credibility score.” A claim can be:

- mathematically true but not formally verified;
- computationally supported but outside a declared enumeration scope;
- correct after narrowing but false in its original form;
- refuted by a minimal witness;
- blocked by missing reproducibility metadata;
- accepted for internal use but not publication-ready.

These are **typed states**, not a single confidence axis.

A suitable state lattice is:

```text
DRAFT
ASSERTED
SUPPORTED
COMPUTATION_REPRODUCED
PROOF_DERIVED
SCOPE_NARROWED
REFUTED
RETRACTED
SUPERSEDED
QUARANTINED
BLOCKED
FORMALLY_CERTIFIED
PUBLICATION_ELIGIBLE
```

The allowed transitions must be policy-controlled, append-only, and attributable.

***

### MCPmed and scientific MCP packs

MCPmed adapts MCP to bioinformatics web services by associating API endpoints with scientific concepts and metadata. It has implementations or templates around services including GEO, STRING, UCSC Cell Browser, and PLSDB, while also proposing “breadcrumbs” for services that are not fully MCP-enabled.[4][5][14][15]

```text
Scientific web service
      │
      ▼
MCP wrapper / metadata layer
      │
      ▼
Tool discovery by LLM agent
      │
      ▼
Structured service call
      │
      ▼
Data / analysis result
```

### What Atlas should borrow

- A capability registry for tools.
- Explicit input and output schemas.
- Versioned service metadata.
- Tool discovery constrained by domain semantics.
- “Breadcrumb” adapters for partially structured external sources.

### Atlas-specific enhancement

An MCP tool call should never be considered evidence merely because it succeeded. Atlas should distinguish:

```text
tool invocation
      ≠
observed result
      ≠
validated result
      ≠
accepted evidence
      ≠
claim promotion
```

A research tool result should enter through a receipt:

```yaml
receipt_id: RUN-2026-09-28-001
tool:
  protocol: mcp
  server: geo-mcp
  version: 1.4.2
activity:
  command: search_datasets
  args_sha256: ...
inputs:
  entity_ids: [...]
outputs:
  artifact_sha256: ...
environment:
  client_version: ...
verification:
  status: OBSERVED
  validators:
    - schema-pass
    - content-hash-pass
claim_links:
  supports:
    - AQ-BIO-EXPR-004
```

Only a later policy transition can turn that observed receipt into admissible support.

***

### Open-Science workbenches

The newest open-source workbenches position themselves as local-first, model-agnostic environments that combine agents, Python/R execution, scientific connectors, reviewer checks, and traceable research artifacts across desktop operating systems.[6][7][8][9]

```text
Desktop / local workspace
      │
      ├── user files
      ├── Python / R execution
      ├── web and database connectors
      ├── model-agnostic agents
      ├── reports / tables / plots
      └── traceable artifacts
```

### What Atlas should borrow

- Local-first default.
- A workspace abstraction.
- Execution receipts for scripts and notebooks.
- Model/provider independence.
- Human review of generated outputs.
- Cross-platform packaging only after the core data model is stable.

### What Atlas should not build first

Do not begin with:

- a desktop shell;
- a multi-agent chat interface;
- model-routing controls;
- notebook replacement;
- broad scientific connector catalog;
- a full visual graph application.

Those are execution and interaction layers. The defensible moat is the registry and policy engine underneath.

Atlas should initially operate as a repository-native CLI/API:

```bash
aq init
aq claim add
aq evidence attach
aq replay claim AQ-COOC-001
aq test negative-controls
aq diff research REV_A REV_B
aq export ro-crate claim AQ-COOC-001
aq verify release
```

A desktop or web surface can later consume the same canonical registry.

***

### ActiveGraph

ActiveGraph describes itself as an event-sourced reactive graph runtime for long-running auditable agentic systems. It models shared beliefs, tasks, evidence, decisions, and dependencies, derived from an append-only event log; it also supports replay, forking, and diffing. Its packs bundle types, behaviors, tools, prompts, policies, fixtures, and UI elements.[10][11][12]

```text
Append-only event stream
      │
      ▼
Shared object graph
      │
      ├── beliefs
      ├── tasks
      ├── evidence
      ├── decisions
      ├── dependencies
      └── policies
                │
                ▼
Reactive behaviors / agents / tools
                │
                ▼
Replay · fork · diff · inspect
```

### Why this is strategically important

This is the most compelling external architecture for Atlas because Atlas also benefits from:

- append-only transitions;
- replayable history;
- policy-mediated actions;
- objects whose state is derived from events;
- durable, inspectable agent activity;
- graph-native dependency and impact analysis.

### Recommended relationship

Do not necessarily build on ActiveGraph at version one. Instead, make Atlas **event-model-compatible** with it.

Atlas can start with JSONL event sourcing:

```text
events/
├── 2026-09-28T00-15-21.claim-created.json
├── 2026-09-28T00-18-08.evidence-attached.json
├── 2026-09-28T00-20-33.replay-observed.json
├── 2026-09-28T00-24-41.claim-promoted.json
└── 2026-09-28T00-29-12.negative-control-registered.json
```

Then, if ActiveGraph proves stable and useful, an Atlas pack can map:

| Atlas object | ActiveGraph-style object |
|---|---|
| Claim | Stateful claim node |
| Evidence item | Provenance/evidence node |
| Execution receipt | Activity/result node |
| Convention profile | Policy/configuration node |
| Negative control | Invariant / regression node |
| Transition proposal | Decision/task node |
| Release gate | Policy evaluation node |

This preserves independence while enabling later runtime integration.

## Provenance substrate

### W3C PROV

W3C PROV provides a solid lowest-common-denominator semantic layer:

$$
\texttt{prov:Entity},
\qquad
\texttt{prov:Activity},
\qquad
\texttt{prov:Agent}.
$$

An entity has fixed aspects, an activity occurs over time and uses or produces entities, and an agent bears responsibility for activities or entities.[16][17][18]

Atlas should map:

| Atlas object | PROV mapping |
|---|---|
| Claim revision | `prov:Entity` |
| Proof document | `prov:Entity` |
| Counterexample witness | `prov:Entity` |
| Script | `prov:Entity` |
| Manifest | `prov:Entity` |
| Reproduction run | `prov:Activity` |
| Human researcher | `prov:Person` / `prov:Agent` |
| AI verifier | `prov:SoftwareAgent` |
| CI runner | `prov:SoftwareAgent` |
| Generated receipt | `prov:Entity` |
| Claim promotion decision | `prov:Activity` with policy metadata |

But PROV should remain **substrate**, not decision logic. It says that a run generated a result; it does not say whether a result is enough to advance a claim from `SUPPORTED` to `ACCEPTED`.

### RO-Crate and Workflow Run Crate

Workflow Run Crate and Provenance Run Crate are strong export/package targets. They represent workflow executions and their associated inputs, outputs, code, tools, parameters, and—in the more detailed provenance profile—individual tool steps and intermediate outputs.[19][20][21][22][23][24]

Atlas should export each accepted claim bundle as:

```text
claim-ro-crate/
├── ro-crate-metadata.json
├── claim.json
├── scope.json
├── convention-profile.yaml
├── evidence/
├── negative-controls/
├── replay/
├── receipt.json
├── environment.lock
└── README.md
```

The important design separation is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{RO-Crate packages evidence. Atlas governs claim state.}
}
$$

RO-Crate validators already support validation against declared profiles, detailed issue reporting, local/ZIP/remote crates, and profile extensions using SHACL and Python. Use an existing validator rather than inventing one.[25][26][27]

## Feature matrix

| Capability | PARNESS | Plato’s Cave | MCPmed | Open-Science workbenches | ActiveGraph | RO-Crate / PROV | AQARION Atlas target |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Local-first operation | Partial / unspecified | Usually web-stack oriented | Service layer | Strong | Deployable/runtime dependent | Package-level | Strong |
| Declarative workflows | Strong | Limited | Endpoint-level | Variable | Behaviors/packs | Descriptive, not orchestration | Strong |
| Full-text PDF extraction | Strong | Strong | No | Variable | No | No | Optional adapter |
| Repository/code indexing | Strong | Limited | No | Workspace-level | Pack-dependent | Package metadata | Strong but secondary |
| Agent tool execution | Strong | Web agents | Strong via MCP | Strong | Strong | No | Strong, receipt-gated |
| Scientific service discovery | Limited | Web search | Strong | Connector-based | Pack-dependent | No | MCP registry adapter |
| Claim graph | Ideas/experiments graph | Core feature | No | Usually weak | Generic beliefs/evidence graph | No | Core feature |
| Explicit theorem/refutation state | No | Credibility-oriented | No | No | Generic policy possible | No | Core feature |
| Immutable negative controls | No | No | No | Rare | Possible but generic | Packageable | Core feature |
| Convention compatibility firewall | No | No | Endpoint semantics only | Rare | Policy possible | No | Core feature |
| Replay contract | Workflow-level | Limited | Tool-call level | Artifact-level | Event replay | Run/package provenance | Claim-level |
| Evidence freshness | Partial | Web-evidence dependent | Service freshness | Artifact history | Event history | Metadata possible | Core policy |
| Promotion / publication policy | No | Scoring/review | No | No | Generic policies | No | Core policy |
| Research semantic diff | No | No | No | File/workspace history | Event diff | Package diff only | Core feature |
| Formal–computational gap visibility | No | No | No | Rare | Generic | No | Core dashboard |
| Exportable provenance standard | Partial | Unclear | MCP metadata | Variable | Custom runtime | Strong | Native export |

## The Atlas architecture

The system should be designed around **three separate graphs**. Do not collapse them.

### 1. Claim graph

Captures mathematical/scientific meaning.

```text
Claim
  ├── statement
  ├── scope
  ├── status
  ├── dependencies
  ├── descendants
  ├── supersedes / corrected-by
  ├── refuted-by
  └── promotion policy
```

Examples:

```text
AQ-COOC-001
AQ-BIP-001
AQ-DEFECT-FOUR-001
AQ-WGRAM-001
AQ-DELTA-RESIDUE-001
```

### 2. Evidence/provenance graph

Captures what was actually run, produced, observed, and attributed.

```text
Artifact → used by → Execution
Execution → generated → Receipt
Receipt → validates → Artifact
Agent → associated with → Execution
Execution → supports → Claim revision
```

This is where PROV and RO-Crate fit.

### 3. Transition/policy graph

Captures what the system permits.

```text
ASSERTED
   │
   ├── direct proof accepted ──► PROOF_DERIVED
   ├── census replayed ────────► COMPUTATION_REPRODUCED
   ├── witness found ──────────► REFUTED
   ├── scope repair ───────────► SCOPE_NARROWED
   ├── stronger statement ─────► SUPERSEDED
   └── missing gate ───────────► BLOCKED
```

The policy graph must reject invalid transitions:

```text
OPEN → PROVED
```

without an admissible proof artifact.

It must reject:

```text
REFUTED → ACCEPTED
```

unless a **new claim ID** is created with a modified statement or scope.

It must reject:

```text
COMPUTATION_REPRODUCED → FORMALLY_CERTIFIED
```

without a formal proof receipt.

## Canonical data model

Use append-only JSONL events plus derived SQLite/DuckDB views.

```text
atlas/
├── registry/
│   ├── claims.jsonl
│   ├── claim_revisions.jsonl
│   ├── evidence.jsonl
│   ├── executions.jsonl
│   ├── receipts.jsonl
│   ├── transitions.jsonl
│   ├── conventions.jsonl
│   ├── negative_controls.jsonl
│   └── edges.jsonl
├── schemas/
│   ├── claim.v1.json
│   ├── evidence.v1.json
│   ├── receipt.v1.json
│   ├── transition.v1.json
│   ├── convention-profile.v1.json
│   ├── negative-control.v1.json
│   └── release-policy.v1.json
├── artifacts/
│   ├── claims/
│   ├── evidence/
│   ├── receipts/
│   └── crates/
├── generated/
│   ├── atlas.db
│   ├── claim-atlas.mmd
│   ├── negative-controls.md
│   ├── release-status.md
│   └── research-diff/
└── policies/
    ├── transition-policy.yaml
    ├── evidence-policy.yaml
    └── publication-policy.yaml
```

### Minimal claim record

```json
{
  "id": "AQ-COOC-001",
  "revision": "2.0.0",
  "kind": "theorem",
  "title": "Defect rank via target co-occurrence components",
  "statement_latex": "\\operatorname{rank}(\\Delta_\\Pi)=m-c(H_\\Pi)",
  "status": "PROOF_DERIVED",
  "scope": {
    "state_space": "finite",
    "dynamics": "deterministic",
    "koopman_convention": "pullback-row",
    "defect": "restricted-(I-P)K|im(P)",
    "field": "rational-or-real",
    "partition_role": "same source/target partition"
  },
  "depends_on": [
    "AQ-OPERATOR-001",
    "AQ-COOC-GRAPH-001",
    "AQ-KERNEL-CONSTRAINT-001"
  ],
  "refutes": [
    "AQ-BIP-001",
    "AQ-NBRIDGE-001"
  ],
  "evidence_policy": "direct_proof_plus_replay",
  "promotion_policy": "no_publication_without_c4",
  "created_at": "2026-09-28T00:00:00Z"
}
```

### Minimal evidence record

```json
{
  "id": "EVID-COOC-CENSUS-001",
  "kind": "exhaustive_census",
  "supports": ["AQ-COOC-001"],
  "scope_compatibility": "exact",
  "manifest_sha256": "…",
  "script_sha256": "…",
  "input_domain": {
    "n_max": 5,
    "maps": "all deterministic maps",
    "partitions": "all canonical set partitions",
    "arithmetic": "exact-rational"
  },
  "outcome": {
    "cases": 293750,
    "violations": 0
  },
  "receipt_id": "RUN-COOC-2026-09-28-001",
  "admissibility": "accepted"
}
```

### Minimal negative-control record

```json
{
  "id": "NC-BIP-001",
  "refutes": "AQ-BIP-001",
  "status": "PERMANENT_NEGATIVE_CONTROL",
  "minimality": {
    "state_count": 2,
    "proof": "enumerated_smaller_domain"
  },
  "witness": {
    "T": [0, 0],
    "partition": [[0], [1]]
  },
  "expected": {
    "rank_defect": 0,
    "cooccurrence_prediction": 0,
    "retired_bipartite_prediction": 1
  },
  "replay": {
    "command": "uv run python negative_controls/nc_bip_001.py",
    "expected_exit": 0
  }
}
```

## Research-state CI

The CI system should evaluate claim semantics, not merely code health.

```yaml
jobs:
  schema:
    name: Validate registry schemas

  graph:
    name: Validate claim/evidence/transition graph integrity

  conventions:
    name: Reject incompatible evidence comparisons

  replay:
    name: Replay deterministic evidence contracts

  negative_controls:
    name: Ensure refuted claims remain refuted

  freshness:
    name: Detect stale scripts, manifests, or receipts

  provenance:
    name: Validate RO-Crate / PROV export

  policy:
    name: Validate claimed status transitions

  release:
    name: Enforce publication and promotion gates
```

### Examples of high-value failures

```text
FAIL AQ-COOC-001:
  current claim scope says pullback-row;
  attached evidence EVID-OLD-007 used pushforward-column.
  Evidence is scope-incompatible.

FAIL AQ-WGRAM-001:
  spectral claim references L_W as an orthonormal Gram matrix;
  convention profile declares raw indicator coordinates.
  Required normalization B^(-1/2)L_WB^(-1/2) absent.

FAIL AQ-BIP-001:
  new document marks the retired formula as "theorem".
  Permanent negative control NC-BIP-001 blocks promotion.

FAIL AQ-DELTA-001:
  reproduction receipt script hash does not match the script now attached
  to the claim revision.

FAIL RELEASE-2026-09:
  formalization channel marked FORMALLY_CERTIFIED without a verified theorem-specific receipt.
```

## Unique integration opportunities

### 1. Claim-state pack for ActiveGraph

A future Atlas–ActiveGraph integration could make claim governance a reusable agent-runtime pack:

```text
aqatlas-pack/
├── Claim
├── ClaimRevision
├── Evidence
├── Receipt
├── ConventionProfile
├── NegativeControl
├── TransitionProposal
├── ReleaseGate
└── behaviors/
    ├── validate_transition
    ├── check_scope_compatibility
    ├── replay_contract
    ├── propagate_refutation
    └── generate_research_diff
```

ActiveGraph’s event sourcing, shared graph, replay, and pack model are a natural foundation for this, but Atlas should first prove its data model with a simpler local JSONL/SQLite implementation.[10][12]

### 2. MCP gateway with admissibility labels

Instead of treating all MCP tools as equally trustworthy, Atlas can classify tool outputs:

```text
DISCOVERY_ONLY
OBSERVED_RESULT
REPRODUCIBLE_RESULT
INDEPENDENTLY_REPLAYED
ADMISSIBLE_EVIDENCE
PUBLICATION_GRADE_EVIDENCE
```

This is particularly important for web/database MCP calls, where live data changes and a successful endpoint response is not necessarily stable or citable evidence.

### 3. RO-Crate claim bundles

Export a separate RO-Crate for each accepted or refuted claim, not only for entire repositories.

That creates a portable unit:

```text
Claim package:
  statement
  scope
  convention profile
  evidence artifacts
  receipt
  counterexamples
  environment lock
  policy status
  provenance graph
```

A paper can then cite claim crates individually rather than asking reviewers to reconstruct an entire monorepo history.

### 4. Status-aware RAG

The RAG layer should never answer from semantic similarity alone. Retrieval should be constrained by:

$$
\operatorname{score}(d,q)
=
\operatorname{semantic}(d,q)
\cdot
\operatorname{statusAdmissibility}(d)
\cdot
\operatorname{scopeCompatibility}(d,q)
\cdot
\operatorname{freshness}(d).
$$

For example, a query about “the rank theorem” should prioritize the current scoped claim and surface killed alternatives under a separate “do not use” heading.

```text
Current theorem:
  AQ-COOC-001

Scope:
  pullback-row, restricted defect, target co-occurrence graph

Do not use:
  AQ-BIP-001 — refuted
  AQ-NBRIDGE-001 — refuted
  AQ-FOUR-DEFECT-001 — retired; identically zero

Formal channel:
  open / not used as current acceptance basis
```

This is a tangible improvement over conventional RAG, where obsolete claims are often retrieved because they are lexically or semantically similar.

### 5. Convention firewall as a portable protocol

The convention profile could become an independent standard-like component:

```yaml
operator:
  koopman_orientation: pullback-row
  matrix_encoding: K[x, T[x]] = 1
  defect_form: restricted-(I-P)K
  ambient_extension: (I-P)KP

projection:
  kind: orthogonal-block-average
  partition_relation: same-source-target

coordinates:
  block_basis: indicators
  coefficient_metric: diag(block_sizes)
  gram_normalization: B^-1/2 L B^-1/2

arithmetic:
  field: rationals
  numerical_tolerance: null

enumeration:
  partition_canonicalization: restricted-growth-string-v1
  transition_encoding: tuple-v1
```

Evidence attachment becomes a type-checking problem:

$$
\boxed{
\text{No comparison, aggregation, or promotion without convention compatibility.}
}
$$

This has potential beyond AQARION in computational physics, numerical linear algebra, ML benchmark reproduction, and formal-methods workflows.

## Recommended build sequence

### Phase 0: write the protocol

Before writing a dashboard, freeze:

- claim schema;
- evidence schema;
- transition schema;
- convention profile;
- negative-control schema;
- status semantics;
- admissibility rules;
- identity/versioning rules;
- immutable-event policy.

The hard design question is not visualization. It is:

> When exactly is a new statement a revision of an old claim, and when must it receive a new claim ID because its scope or truth conditions changed?

A practical rule:

| Change | Same claim revision? | New claim ID? |
|---|---:|---:|
| Better proof of identical statement and scope | Yes | No |
| New replay receipt | Yes | No |
| Corrected wording with unchanged semantics | Yes | No |
| Narrowed hypothesis | No | Yes |
| Changed operator convention | No | Yes |
| Changed enumeration universe | Usually no | Yes |
| Counterexample refutes prior statement | Prior claim becomes `REFUTED` | Replacement gets new ID |
| Stronger conclusion | No | Yes |
| Formal proof of existing statement | Yes, new evidence | No |

### Phase 1: repository-native command line

Build only these commands:

```bash
aq init
aq claim add
aq claim show AQ-COOC-001
aq evidence attach AQ-COOC-001 evidence.json
aq replay claim AQ-COOC-001
aq test negatives
aq verify registry
aq diff research REV_A REV_B
aq export crate AQ-COOC-001
```

A successful first release needs no LLM, no desktop app, and no graph database.

### Phase 2: one complete AQARION demonstration

Use exactly four claim clusters:

1. Operator convention and four-factor retirement.
2. Target-cooccurrence rank theorem.
3. Bipartite bridge refutation.
4. Weighted Gram normalization correction.

This compact set demonstrates:

- accepted theorem;
- convention repair;
- evidence replay;
- permanent negative control;
- scope-aware claim revision;
- spectral normalization warning;
- research diff;
- RO-Crate export.

### Phase 3: RAG and agent interfaces

Add:

- evidence-aware retrieval;
- MCP tool adapters;
- research-state summary generation;
- claim-transition proposal generation;
- mandatory human/policy approval.

The agent should be allowed to propose:

```text
Transition proposal:
  AQ-COOC-001
  SUPPORTED → COMPUTATION_REPRODUCED
  Evidence:
    RUN-2026-09-28-042
  Reason:
    independent replay matches expected invariant
```

The agent must not be allowed to enact that transition without policy validation and, where configured, human approval.

### Phase 4: visual atlas and workbench adapters

Only then add:

- Graphviz/Mermaid generated diagrams;
- Cytoscape.js browser;
- local desktop workbench integration;
- ActiveGraph pack;
- scientific MCP catalog;
- multi-project atlas;
- publication dossier generator.

## What not to build

Avoid these early failures:

- A generic “AI scientist” chat application.
- A provenance system that has no claim semantics.
- A claim graph that does not store exact statements and scope.
- A dashboard of confidence scores that hides categorical refutation.
- A graph database before local registry queries become inadequate.
- An MCP server catalog before the claim/evidence system can consume receipts correctly.
- A generic note-taking/RAG tool branded as “research governance.”
- A formal-proof workflow as the required core of every claim.

## Bottom line

The mature product thesis is:

$$
\boxed{
\textbf{AQARION Atlas}
=
\text{a local-first claim-state compiler and evidence-policy engine}
}
$$

with:

$$
\boxed{
\text{replayable provenance from RO-Crate/PROV,}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{interoperable execution through MCP,}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{durable event history inspired by ActiveGraph,}
}
$$

and, critically,

$$
\boxed{
\text{first-class scope repair, refutation, and promotion governance.}
}
$$

PARNESS is the closest workflow-and-knowledge-harness comparison; Plato’s Cave is the closest paper-claim verification comparison; MCPmed is the clearest scientific-tool interoperability comparison; Open-Science workbenches are the likely execution surface; ActiveGraph is the most relevant durable runtime; and RO-Crate/PROV are the correct provenance/export substrates.[1][2][4][6][10][16][19]

The differentiator is not “more agents” or “better RAG.” It is the ability to say—mechanically, reproducibly, and conservatively—what a research project is permitted to claim right now, why, under what conventions, and what known counterexamples permanently constrain the search space.

4. Inline deliverable: verification script

verification/verify_pullback_join.py (the exact logic executed above, n≤3 in this turn; extend to n≤5 on adequate hardware):
"""Exhaustive check: join of backward-stable equivalences is backward-stable.
Counts use the 1/6/51 convention. Negative control for preimage distributivity included."""
import itertools

def partitions_of(n):
    elems = list(range(n))
    def rec(rem):
        if not rem: yield []; return
        f, rest = rem[0], rem[1:]
        for p in rec(rest):
            yield [[f]] + p
            for i in range(len(p)):
                q = [list(b) for b in p]; q[i] = q[i] + [f]; yield q
    seen = set()
    for p in rec(elems):
        k = tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(b)) for b in p))
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k); yield [list(b) for b in k]

def rel(p, n):
    R = [[False]*n for _ in range(n)]
    for b in p:
        for x in b:
            for y in b: R[x][y] = True
    return R

def pb(R, T, n): return [[R[T[i]][T[j]] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
def le(A, B, n): return all(not A[i][j] or B[i][j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n))
def join(R, S, n):
    U = [[R[i][j] or S[i][j] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    ch = True
    while ch:
        ch = False
        for k in range(n):
            for i in range(n):
                if U[i][k]:
                    for j in range(n):
                        if U[k][j] and not U[i][j]: U[i][j] = True; ch = True
    return U

for n in (1, 2, 3):
    parts = list(partitions_of(n)); rels = [rel(p, n) for p in parts]
    viol, stable = 0, 0
    for T in itertools.product(range(n), repeat=n):
        st = [R for R in rels if le(pb(R, T, n), R, n)]
        stable += len(st)
        for i in range(len(st)):
            for j in range(i, len(st)):
                J = join(st[i], st[j], n)
                if not le(pb(J, T, n), J, n): viol += 1
    print(f"n={n} stable={stable} violations={viol}")
    assert viol == 0
negative control
n = 3; T = (0,0,1)
E, F = rel([[0,2],[1]], n), rel([[0],[1,2]], n)
assert not le(pb(join(E,F,n),T,n), join(pb(E,T,n),pb(F,T,n),n), n)
print("NEGATIVE CONTROL CONFIRMED: preimage distributivity refuted")

2. aqverify/hashing.py
from future import annotations
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

def sha256_file(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(65536), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()

def sha256_text(text: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

def canonical_json(value: Any) -> str:
    return json.dumps(value, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False)
3. aqverify/claim.py
from future import annotations
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

REQUIRED = ("schema", "id", "text", "scope")
SCHEMA = "aqarion.claim.v1"

def load_claim(path: Path) -> dict[str, Any]:
    data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise ValueError("claim root must be a JSON object")
    for key in REQUIRED:
        if key not in data:
            raise ValueError(f"claim missing required field: {key}")
    if data["schema"]!= SCHEMA:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported claim schema: {data['schema']!r}")
    if not isinstance(data["scope"], dict) or not isinstance(data["scope"].get("statement"), str):
        raise ValueError("claim.scope.statement must be a string")
    return data
4. aqverify/audit.py
from future import annotations
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

UNIVERSAL_PATTERNS = (
    r"\bfor all\b", r"\bfor every\b", r"\bevery\b",
    r"\buniversal\b", r"\bfor arbitrary\b", r"\bany finite\b",
)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Finding:
    code: str
    severity: str
    message: str

def detect_universal_language(text: str) -> list[Finding]:
    for pattern in UNIVERSAL_PATTERNS:
        if re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE):
            return [Finding("UNIVERSAL_LANGUAGE", "INFO",
                "Universal language detected. A bounded computation does not establish this scope.")]
    return []

def scope_mismatch(claim_text: str, exhaustive: bool, domain: str | None) -> bool:
    if not detect_universal_language(claim_text):
        return False
    if not exhaustive:
        return True
    bounded = bool(re.search(r"\bfinite\b|\bbounded\b|\bn\s*[<≤=]|\bsize\s*[<≤]", domain or "", re.IGNORECASE))
    return not bounded
5. aqverify/receipt.py
from future import annotations
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any
from.hashing import sha256_file

def make_audit_receipt(claim: dict[str, Any], claim_path: Path, findings: list[str]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "schema": "aqarion.receipt.v1",
        "receipt_id": f"{claim['id']}-audit-receipt",
        "claim": {"id": claim["id"], "text": claim["text"], "scope": claim["scope"]["statement"]},
        "source": {"path": str(claim_path), "sha256": sha256_file(claim_path),
                   "input_identity": sha256_file(claim_path)},
        "method": {"type": "metadata-audit", "command": None,
                   "independent_reconstruction": False, "arithmetic": "not-applicable"},
        "coverage": {"exhaustive": False, "cases_tested": 0, "targeted": False,
                     "randomized": False, "random_seed": None},
        "adversarial": {"boundary_cases": [], "negative_controls": [],
                        "counterexamples": [], "mutations": []},
        "result": {"status": "AUDIT_COMPLETE", "failures": 0, "mismatches": 0, "findings": findings},
        "evidence_boundary": [
            "This receipt records a metadata audit.",
            "No experiment was executed.",
            "No proof is implied.",
            "No claim status was promoted.",
        ],
        "promotion": {"allowed": False, "reason": "A metadata audit alone cannot establish a claim."},
    }

def write_receipt(receipt: dict[str, Any], output: Path) -> Path:
    output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output.write_text(json.dumps(receipt, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    return output
6. aqverify/cli.py
from future import annotations
import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from.audit import detect_universal_language, scope_mismatch
from.claim import load_claim
from.receipt import make_audit_receipt, write_receipt

def cmd_audit(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    claim = load_claim(Path(args.claim))
    findings = detect_universal_language(claim["text"])
    mismatch = scope_mismatch(claim["text"], exhaustive=False, domain=claim["scope"].get("domain"))
    print("AQARION VERIFY")
    print(f"Claim: {claim['id']}")
    for f in findings:
        print(f"[{f.severity}] {f.code}: {f.message}")
    print("[WARN] SCOPE_MISMATCH: universal language with no exhaustive proof." if mismatch
          else "[INFO] No deterministic scope mismatch detected.")
    print("STATUS: AUDIT_COMPLETE")
    print("PROMOTION: BLOCKED")
    return 0

def cmd_receipt(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    claim_path = Path(args.claim)
    claim = load_claim(claim_path)
    findings = [f.code for f in detect_universal_language(claim["text"])]
    receipt = make_audit_receipt(claim, claim_path, findings)
    output = write_receipt(receipt, Path(args.output))
    print(output)
    return 0

def cmd_validate_receipt(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    receipt = json.loads(Path(args.receipt).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    required = {"schema","receipt_id","claim","source","method","coverage",
                "adversarial","result","evidence_boundary","promotion"}
    missing = sorted(required.difference(receipt))
    if missing:
        print(f"INVALID: missing receipt keys: {', '.join(missing)}")
        return 2
    if receipt.get("schema")!= "aqarion.receipt.v1":
        print("INVALID: unsupported receipt schema")
        return 2
    print("VALID: aqarion.receipt.v1")
    return 0

def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="aq-verify")
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    audit = subparsers.add_parser("audit")
    audit.add_argument("claim")
    audit.set_defaults(handler=cmd_audit)
    receipt = subparsers.add_parser("receipt")
    receipt.add_argument("claim")
    receipt.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    receipt.set_defaults(handler=cmd_receipt)
    validate = subparsers.add_parser("validate-receipt")
    validate.add_argument("receipt")
    validate.set_defaults(handler=cmd_validate_receipt)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    return args.handler(args)

if name == "main":
    sys.exit(main())

11. README.md
AQARION VERIFY

Evidence and adversarial verification infrastructure for AI-assisted research.

Core principle

Evidence does not inherit authority from language. "proved", "verified",
"certified", "exhaustive" are claims to audit, not evidence.

Status axes (not one enum)

claim_status: OPEN / REFUTED / RETRACTED
mathematical_status: PROOF_CANDIDATE / PAPER_PROVED / REFUTED
computational_status: UNTESTED / VERIFIED_FINITE / COUNTEREXAMPLE_REPLAYED
formal_status: OPEN / PROVED
governance_status: BLOCKED / HISTORICAL_PRESERVED
promotion_allowed: bool

Rule: an execution does not change a mathematical status by itself.

Use

pip install -e.
aq-verify audit examples/claim.json
aq-verify receipt examples/claim.json --output receipt.json
aq-verify validate-receipt receipt.json

License

Apache-2.0.
Run: pip install -e. && python -m pytest -q && aq-verify audit examples/claim.json

Frozen ledger 2026-09-27: kernel/rank + 166483 | pair-δ + 119/119 | two-block δ PROVED + 102504 | GCD closure CLOSED | support formula PROVED | T10 KILLED | old δ KILLED | C17 SUSPENDED | transport s_T = s_0 + Δ + m_T | CI BLOCKED | C4 BLOCKED | publication BLOCKED | Lean OPEN[T][C2]

## Product correctness

The v0.1 restraint is correct. It should only:

```bash

aq-verify receipt claim.json --output receipt.json

```

The output should say:

```text
STATUS: AUDIT_COMPLETE
PROMOTION: BLOCKED
```

not:

```text
STATUS: VERIFIED
```

A metadata audit can verify that a claim file has required fields and can flag universal language; it cannot verify the truth of the claim or even execute its proposed experiment.

## Core model

Your proposed hierarchy is sound:

$$
\text{Session}
\rightarrow
\text{Research Event}
\rightarrow
\text{Knowledge Node}
\rightarrow
\text{Claim/Evidence/Artifact}
\rightarrow
\text{Governance}.
$$

The essential addition is indeed:

```text
search_space_effect
```

because AQARION research often progresses by eliminating attractive but false formulations.

Use only these controlled values:

```text
EXPANDS
NARROWS
ELIMINATES
REFUTES
REFORMULATES
CONNECTS
NO_CHANGE
```

The distinction matters:

| Effect | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `EXPANDS` | Introduces a new plausible line of inquiry |
| `NARROWS` | Reduces admissible hypotheses or proof routes |
| `ELIMINATES` | Removes a route after a theorem or exhaustive bounded result |
| `REFUTES` | Supplies a counterexample to a claim as stated |
| `REFORMULATES` | Replaces an ill-posed or vacuous formulation with a precise one |
| `CONNECTS` | Establishes a dependency, equivalence, or bridge between branches |
| `NO_CHANGE` | Reproduction or audit confirms status without changing the search space |

## Status axes

Do not flatten the current ledger into a single `CLOSED` field. Use orthogonal state:

```json
{
  "claim_status": "OPEN",
  "mathematical_status": "PAPER_PROOF_CANDIDATE",
  "computational_status": "VERIFIED_FINITE",
  "formal_status": "OPEN",
  "governance_status": "BLOCKED",
  "promotion_allowed": false
}
```

For a refuted claim:

```json
{
  "claim_status": "REFUTED",
  "mathematical_status": "REFUTED",
  "computational_status": "COUNTEREXAMPLE_REPLAYED",
  "formal_status": "NOT_APPLICABLE",
  "governance_status": "HISTORICAL_PRESERVED",
  "promotion_allowed": false
}
```

Thus “closed” can mean only a clearly typed closure:

```text
CLOSED_BY_PAPER_PROOF
CLOSED_BY_COUNTEREXAMPLE
CLOSED_FOR_DECLARED_FINITE_DOMAIN
CLOSED_AS_SUPERSEDED
```

Never use a bare green checkmark as a status.

## Standards boundary

The proposed integration is correct:

$$
\text{AQARION lineage semantics}
\longrightarrow
\text{W3C PROV relations}
\longrightarrow
\text{RO-Crate 1.3 / Workflow Run RO-Crate export}.

W3C PROV models entities, activities, agents, and derivation relationships; AQARION can supply domain-level semantics such as claim status, defeater, search-space effect, promotion gate, and evidence-boundary interpretation. RO-Crate 1.3 is appropriate for packaging the resulting research object and its linked metadata.[1][2]

Do not make AQARION replace those standards. Use an export mapping:

|---|---|---|

| Proof note | `prov:Entity` | File |
| Execution receipt | `prov:Entity` | File |
| Verification run | `prov:Activity` | Workflow run / action |
| Human reviewer | `prov:Agent` | Person/Organization |
| AI proposal | `prov:Agent` with restricted authority | SoftwareApplication/Agent |
| Refutation witness | `prov:Entity` | FileDataset |
| Claim transition | Qualified derivation/activity | Contextual entity or profile extension |

RUN REPORT — 2026-09-27 (continued work)

1. Derived: uniform stabilization bound for pullback closure — NEW

Theorem (AQ-DYN-PULL-CLOSURE-BOUND-001, proof-derived). Let Φ⁻(E) = E ∨ T⁻¹(E) on a finite set X, |X| = n. Iterate E₀ = E, E_{k+1} = Φ⁻(E_k). Then the sequence stabilizes in at most n − 1 strict steps.

Proof. Φ⁻ is monotone and inflationary (E ≤ Φ⁻(E)). If Φ⁻(E) > E strictly, then E ∨ T⁻¹(E) is strictly coarser than E, so the number of blocks strictly decreases by ≥ 1. Block count is an integer in [1, n]. Hence at most n − 1 strict increases before a fixed point. A fixed point satisfies T⁻¹(E) ≤ E, i.e. is backward-stable. ∎

Why it matters: this closes the "finite stabilization" gap that was previously marked structural-but-unbounded. Combined with the join theorem (arbitrary joins of backward-stable equivalences are backward-stable), the least backward-stable equivalence above E exists and is reached by this iteration. No distributivity assumption used.

Status: PROOF-DERIVED (paper proof above, 6 lines). Lean: OPEN. This is the single most important new item this turn.

2. Computed: n=4 exhaustive pullback-join — EXECUTED

Sandbox run this turn, exact integer arithmetic:
n=4: maps=256, partitions=15, stable_instances=592, join_pairs=1276, violations=0
Matches the 592/1276 convention counts from the earlier census (not the 1/6/51 per-distinct-relation convention — conventions not merged). Combined with prior n≤3 runs: zero violations across all tested domains.

Status: [SUP] computational support only. Does not promote the theorem; the proof in §1/earlier report is the mathematical evidence. Lean: OPEN. Promotion: FALSE.

Searched for prior art on "pullback-stable / backward-stable equivalence under finite deterministic map, join closure". No standard textbook or arXiv source matching this exact formulation surfaced. Closest live source remains AQARION's own certification/pullback/kernel_pair_correction.md, which records the kernel-pair form T⁻¹(E) = ker(q_E ∘ T) and marks general join-stability open. Related adjacent areas (partition lattices, bisimulation, forward congruences) exist but state the forward direction E ≤ T⁻¹(E), which is a different condition.

Claim: novelty not asserted over the literature; only that this session's search returned no prior source for the join theorem in backward form. The stabilization bound (§1) is, to the same search depth, new.

1. Derivation (locked definitions)

Let Π={B_1..B_m}, (Pf)(x)=|B_r|^{-1}Σ_{y∈B_r}f(y) for x∈B_r, (Kf)(x)=f(Tx), D=(I-P)KP.

Constraint graph G^con: vertices = blocks; q ~ q' iff some source block B_r contains x,x' with T(x)∈B_q, T(x')∈B_{q'} (each source block induces a clique on reached targets). This is not the ordinary directed quotient graph.

Support formula (entrywise, exact):
D_ij = [1_{T(i)∈B_q} − V_{rq}] / |B_q|, i∈B_r, j∈B_q
V_{rq} = |{x∈B_r : T(x)∈B_q}| / |B_r|
Hence D_ij ≠ 0 iff T(i)∈B_q and 0 < V_{rq} < 1. The quotient graph records only V_{rq}>0; it loses the V_{rq}=1 vs fractional distinction. That's exactly why T10 died.

Rank theorem: DΦv=0 iff v_q/|B_q| is constant on components of G^con, so dim ker(DΦ)=c(G^con), rank(D)=m−c(G^con).

3. Literature search — honest crosswalk

Recent Koopman literature (EDMD/projection-error framing, e.g. arxiv 2410.02766, 2511.06063) treats the projection of the Koopman operator onto a finite subspace and the resulting approximation error ‖K(v) − proj(K(v))‖ as a central object — this is the right neighborhood for positioning D=(I-P)KP as an exact finite-state invariance defect, but none of it proves the AQARION identities.
Matrix-weighted incidence theory is the correct analogy for the T10 kill: weights (V_{rq}, block sizes) change behavior the unweighted graph can't see.
No prior source found for the exact formulas above in this form; I am not claiming novelty, only that the search returned AQARION's own checkpoints as the closest match.

4. Brainstorm — the important next thing

Target: matrix-valued persistence for r ≥ 3 blocks.

The two-block case is solved because rank(D)≤1 collapses everything to the scalar autocorrelation C_m. For r≥3, D has transverse dimension r−1 and DK^mD is genuinely matrix-valued. The natural conjecture:
DK^mD = 0 ⟺ (UᵀK^{m+1}U) = (UᵀKU)(UᵀK^mU)
where U is an orthonormal basis of the transverse subspace (I-P)ℝ^n (dimension r−1), making the right side an (r−1)×(r−1) matrix identity rather than a scalar one.

Derive the block-matrix form of UᵀK^mU in terms of the r×r transition statistics V and block sizes.

```python
def test_audit_receipt_never_promotes(tmp_path):
    claim_path = tmp_path / "claim.json"
    claim_path.write_text(
        """
{
  "schema": "aqarion.claim.v1",
  "id": "EX-PROMOTION-001",
  "text": "For every input n, X halts.",
  "scope": {
    "statement": "For every input n, X halts.",
    "domain": "all inputs",
    "quantifiers": ["universal"]
  }
}
""".strip()
    )

    claim = load_claim(claim_path)
    receipt = make_audit_receipt(claim, claim_path, [])

    assert receipt["promotion"]["allowed"] is False
    assert receipt["promotion"]["reason"]
    assert "No proof is implied." in receipt["evidence_boundary"]
```

That test is more important than additional display/UI tests because it protects the central governance boundary.

## Mandatory policy test

The proposed test is exactly the right next change. It should inspect the actual generated receipt rather than test a hand-assembled dictionary.

```python
def test_receipt_generation_cannot_promote(tmp_path):
    claim_path = tmp_path / "claim.json"
    output_path = tmp_path / "receipt.json"

    claim_path.write_text(
        """
{
  "schema": "aqarion.claim.v1",
  "id": "EX-PROMOTION-NEGATIVE-CONTROL-001",
  "text": "For every input n, process X halts.",
  "scope": {
    "statement": "For every input n, process X halts.",
    "domain": "all inputs",
    "quantifiers": ["universal"]
  }
}
""".strip(),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    result = runner.invoke(
        app,
        [
            "receipt",
            str(claim_path),
            "--output",
            str(output_path),
        ],
    )

    assert result.exit_code == 0

    receipt = json.loads(output_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    assert receipt["promotion"]["allowed"] is False
    assert receipt["promotion"]["status"] in {
        "BLOCKED",
        "NOT_AUTHORIZED",
        "AUDIT_ONLY",
    }
```

Add a second negative-control test: no user-supplied field may override the invariant.

```python
def test_claim_cannot_request_or_force_promotion(tmp_path):
    claim_path = tmp_path / "claim.json"
    output_path = tmp_path / "receipt.json"

    claim_path.write_text(
        """
{
  "schema": "aqarion.claim.v1",
  "id": "EX-PROMOTION-ESCALATION-001",
  "text": "This claim is proved.",
  "promotion": {
    "allowed": true,
    "requested_by": "untrusted-input"
  }
}
""".strip(),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    result = runner.invoke(
        app,
        [
            "receipt",
            str(claim_path),
            "--output",
            str(output_path),
        ],
    )

    assert result.exit_code != 0 or (
        json.loads(output_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        ["promotion"]["allowed"]
        is False
    )
```

Prefer rejection of unrecognized promotion fields over silently accepting them. A strict schema prevents future accidental privilege escalation.

## Minimal v0.1 boundary

The product boundary is coherent:

```text
aqverify v0.1
├── audit
├── receipt
└── validate-receipt
```

It should not accept an “execute this arbitrary command” option, a shell field, a workflow field, or a tool URL that could silently change this boundary.

The product claims should remain narrowly phrased:

- “Parses and audits claim metadata.”
- “Records declared evidence boundaries.”
- “Produces non-promotional receipts.”
- “Validates receipt structure and immutable non-promotion policy.”

Avoid:

- “Verifies claims.”
- “Certifies mathematics.”
- “Reproduces experiments.”
- “Runs formal proofs.”
- “Validates CI.”
- “Establishes provenance truth.”

The distinction is especially important because provenance metadata records lineage and activities; it does not independently prove that a mathematical statement is true.[1][2]

## Definitions locked

Let the partition blocks be:

$$
\Pi=\{B_1,\dots,B_m\},
$$

with block-averaging projection:

$$
(Pf)(x)
=
\frac{1}{|B_r|}
\sum_{y\in B_r}f(y),
\qquad x\in B_r.
$$

Let:

$$
K_{i,T(i)}=1,
\qquad
D=(I-P)KP.
$$

For $$i\in B_r$$ and $$j\in B_q$$, define the block transition proportion:

$$
V_{rq}
=
\frac{
|\{x\in B_r:T(x)\in B_q\}|
}{
|B_r|
}.
$$

Then the frozen support formula is:

$$
\boxed{
D_{ij}
=
\frac{
\mathbf 1_{\{T(i)\in B_q\}}-V_{rq}
}{
|B_q|
}.
}
$$

This formula has the correct qualitative consequence:

$$
D_{ij}\ne0
$$

precisely when the membership of $$T(i)$$ in $$B_q$$ differs from the block-average transition frequency $$V_{rq}$$. More explicitly:

$$
D_{ij}\ne0
\iff
\begin{cases}
T(i)\in B_q,\quad V_{rq}<1,\\
\text{or}\\
T(i)\notin B_q,\quad V_{rq}>0.
\end{cases}
$$

That is slightly broader than the one-sided condition:

$$
T(i)\in B_q\land 0<V_{rq}<1.
$$

The latter describes nonzero entries for target blocks that contain $$T(i)$$, but it misses the corresponding negative entries when:

$$
T(i)\notin B_q
\quad\text{and}\quad
0<V_{rq}<1.
$$

For a mixed row-block transition, both kinds of entries occur:

- positive coefficients in reached target blocks;
- negative coefficients in unreached target blocks that are reached by other members of the same source block.

So the support statement should be frozen in its full two-sided form:

$$
\boxed{
D_{ij}\ne0
\iff
\mathbf 1_{\{T(i)\in B_q\}}\ne V_{rq}.
}
$$

Equivalently:

$$
\boxed{
D_{ij}\ne0
\iff
0<V_{rq}<1.
}
$$

for every $$j\in B_q$$, provided $$i\in B_r$$. The distinction is that, once $$V_{rq}$$ is strictly fractional, every $$i\in B_r$$ contributes a nonzero value in every column $$j\in B_q$$; the sign depends on whether that particular state maps into $$B_q$$.

This is exactly the mechanism that kills the old T10 “support determined only by quotient graph” claim:

$$
V_{rq}>0
$$

records only existence of a block-to-block transition, while support depends on whether:

$$
V_{rq}=1,
\qquad
0<V_{rq}<1,
\qquad
\text{or }V_{rq}=0.
$$

An ordinary quotient digraph cannot distinguish deterministic block transition from a fractional split.

## Important correction to the support interpretation

The ledger’s displayed formula is good. The verbal equivalence should be adjusted before freezing.

Do **not** retain:

$$
D_{ij}\ne0
\iff
T(i)\in B_q\land0<V_{rq}<1.
$$

Use:

$$
\boxed{
D_{ij}\ne0
\iff
\mathbf1_{\{T(i)\in B_q\}}\ne V_{rq}.
}
$$

Or, split by sign:

$$
D_{ij}>0
\iff
T(i)\in B_q
\ \land\
V_{rq}<1,
$$

$$
D_{ij}<0
\iff
T(i)\notin B_q
\ \land\
V_{rq}>0.
$$

This makes the T10 negative control stronger and prevents a future false “support formula” refutation caused only by an incomplete support characterization.

## Kernel-rank theorem

The frozen claim should retain the exact graph dependency:

$$
\dim\ker(D\Phi)=c(G^{\mathrm{con}}),
$$

and therefore:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(D)=m-c(G^{\mathrm{con}}),
$$

where:

- $$m$$ is the number of partition blocks;
- $$\Phi$$ is the block-constant embedding;
- $$G^{\mathrm{con}}$$ is the locked bipartite target-coincidence constraint graph;
- $$c(G^{\mathrm{con}})$$ is the number of connected components of that graph.

The qualifier is essential: this is not a theorem about an arbitrary quotient graph, a simple block-transition digraph, or a graph formed only by nonzero $$V_{rq}$$ entries unless those graph definitions are proven equivalent to the locked constraint graph in the relevant setting.

Your proposed status remains correct:

## The $$r\ge3$$ conjecture

The proposed conjecture:

$$
DK^mD=0
\iff
U^\top K^{m+1}U
=
(U^\top KU)(U^\top K^mU)
$$

is correctly marked `OPEN_CONJECTURE` and `UNTESTED`.

The two-block proof cannot simply generalize because the key collapse is scalar:

$$
D=uv^\top
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
DK^mD
=
\bigl(v^\top K^mu\bigr)D.
$$

For rank greater than one, write:

$$
D=UV^\top.
$$

Then:

$$
DK^mD
=
U\left(V^\top K^mU\right)V^\top.
$$

Vanishing requires the entire middle matrix to vanish only when $$U$$ and $$V$$ have the necessary full-column-rank properties. Even then, the proposed matrix identity must be derived from the actual $$U,V,P,K$$ definitions; it is not an automatic analogue of the rank-one formula.

So the correct next move is exactly the one you state:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Falsification first: test }r=3,\ n\le5
\text{ with exact rational arithmetic.}
}
$$

Do not add any “derived” or “analytic” label to this conjecture yet.
